content: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA), previously referred to as Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis, is defined by the American Rheumatism Association as the presence of chronic, seronegative, and peripheral arthritis occurring before the age of 16, lasting for at least three months, and after excluding other potential causes. In polyarticular and systemic onset forms of JIA, symptoms such as chest pain, chest discomfort, and shortness of breath may be observed. Cardiac involvement in JIA is often subclinical, initially presenting as early diastolic dysfunction. Over time, this may progress to symptomatic stages with systolic dysfunction and heart failure, which are typically late findings. Abnormal diastolic function of the left ventricle has also been reported in JIA. When cardiac involvement occurs, it is the second leading cause of mortality in JIA, affecting approximately 7% of cases. Cardiac manifestations may include pericarditis, aortitis, coronary vasculitis, valvulitis (endocarditis), conduction system abnormalities, pulmonary hypertension, and myocarditis. These cardiac complications may arise due to disease progression or as a result of medical treatments. The causes of abnormal diastolic parameters in JIA are multifactorial and may result from cumulative effects of conditions such as pericarditis (with or without pericardial effusion), hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy, cardiotoxic therapies (e.g., cyclosporine, gold salts, D-penicillamine, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine), steroid-induced hypertension, secondary amyloidosis, and vascular stiffness due to vasculitis. Classification of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis 1. Oligoarticular (Pauciarticular) Onset JIA (40-60% of cases): This subtype is more common in girls, with a female-to-male ratio of 5:1. The peak age of onset is around 2 years. During the first six months, four or fewer joints are affected, often asymmetrically. Commonly involved joints include the knees, and less frequently, the ankles and wrists. The arthritis is often transient, rarely destructive, and radiologically insignificant. Approximately 75% of patients test positive for antinuclear antibodies (ANA). Systemic signs are rare, but there is a high risk of uveitis. 2. Polyarticular Onset JIA (20-40% of cases): This subtype is also more common in girls, with a female-to-male ratio of 3:1. The peak age of onset is around 3 years. Five or more joints are affected within the first six months, often involving the small joints of the hands and, less frequently, larger joints such as the knees, ankles, or wrists. Arthritis may be acute or chronic and is destructive in approximately 15% of cases. Rheumatoid factor (IgM form) is present in 10% of children in this subgroup and is associated with subcutaneous nodules, joint erosions, and a poor prognosis. Around 40% of patients test positive for ANA. Systemic symptoms, such as anorexia, anemia, and growth retardation, are moderate. There is an intermediate risk of uveitis. 3. Systemic Onset JIA (10-20% of cases): This subtype occurs equally in boys and girls and can present at any age. Symmetric polyarthritis is present and may be destructive in 25% of cases. Joints commonly involved include the hands, wrists, feet, ankles, elbows, knees, hips, shoulders, cervical spine, and jaw. ANA positivity is observed in only 10% of patients. Systemic features include fever (high in the evening and normal in the morning), macular rash, leukocytosis, lymphadenopathy, and hepatomegaly. Serositis and cardiac involvement, such as pericarditis and myocarditis, may also occur. Other findings include pleuritis, splenomegaly, and abdominal pain, though these are less common. There is a low risk of uveitis. Rarely, aortic cusp thickening and mild mitral insufficiency may be observed in polyarticular forms of JIA. Atrial flutter may also manifest following valve involvement. Diagnosis of Cardiac Involvement 1. Electrocardiography (ECG): Non-specific T wave changes, such as biphasic or negative T waves, may be observed. Pericarditis secondary to JIA can present with characteristic ECG changes associated with pericarditis. 2. Echocardiography: Pericardial effusion can be accurately detected through echocardiographic examination, even in latent stages. In some cases, the left ventricular diastolic diameter may be reduced. Treatment The primary goal of medical therapy in JIA is to reduce pain. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the most commonly used agents. Aspirin, at doses of 75-90 mg/kg/day, is frequently prescribed. Higher doses are generally well-tolerated in younger children. The medication should be administered four times daily with meals. Occasionally, some children may develop elevated liver enzymes, though overt liver disease is extremely rare. There is a recognized association between aspirin use and Reye's syndrome, particularly in the context of viral illnesses. Therefore, children should be immunized against influenza and possibly varicella to mitigate this risk. Prognosis Cardiac function should be evaluated annually through echocardiographic examinations during follow-up. The prognosis for pericarditis is generally favorable if complications such as cardiac tamponade or constrictive pericarditis do not develop.
